name: Nanzhao and Dali kingdoms
summary: Kingdoms in Yunnan, south-west China: Nanzhao (738–902) and the Kingdom of Dali (937–1253), conquered by the Mongols.

knownFor.label: Tea Horse Road
knownFor.note: Trade route through Yunnan to Tibet.

location.value: Yunnan in China, with capitals in modern Dali City and its core around Lake Erhai.

terrain.value: High mountains and deep river gorges, with fertile lake basins such as Erhai and Dian (Kunming).

climate.value: A mild highland climate with warm days, cool nights and a summer rainy season.

resources.value: Rice land in the lake basins, horses, salt from brine wells, and forest products.

disasters.value: Frequent earthquakes in the mountains of Yunnan.

population.value: No total is given; most people were the more sinicised Baiman, and the ruling class was mostly Wuman.

urbanisation.value: Walled capitals beside Erhai Lake, first Taihe and then Yangjumie (Dali), and Tuodong (Kunming).

disease.value: Malaria in the hot river valleys; the Chinese feared the region’s “miasma”.

migration.value: Captives and craftsmen were brought from Sichuan after raids, such as the attack on Chengdu (829).

economicBase.value: In 754 Nanzhao gained the salt marshes of Yanyuan County; the page does not describe rice farming or horse breeding as its base.

tradeRoutes.value: Routes linking Sichuan with Burma and India; horses and tea were traded along what later became the Tea Horse Road.

wealth.value: Wealth came from horses, salt and plunder; Dali’s horses were prized in Song China.

moneyAndTax.value: Cowrie shells, salt and cloth were used as money; farmers owed grain and labour.

inequality.value: A ruling aristocracy of great families above farmers, slaves and conquered peoples.

governmentType.value: A kingdom: Piluoge united the six zhaos in 737 and the Tang gave him the title Prince of Yunnan in 738; Nanzhao’s own dynasty ended in 902 when Zheng Maisi killed the royal family; Duan Siping founded the Dali Kingdom in 937. The page does not give the Mongol conquest of 1253.

keyRulers.value: In 738 the Tang granted Piluoge the name Meng Guiyi and title Prince of Yunnan after he united the Six Zhaos; in 751 a Tang attack was defeated in the Tianbao War; Duan Siping seized power in 937 and founded the Dali Kingdom.

succession.value: Hereditary in the royal family; in Dali the Gao family of chief ministers held much real power.

stability.value: Nanzhao ended when a minister seized the throne (902); after short-lived dynasties, the Duan family ruled Dali for three centuries.

eliteConflict.value: Not well recorded; dynasties changed several times.

armyAndTech.value: Strong armies of hill warriors and cavalry, with fortified mountain towns.

majorWars.value: The Tang attacked with 80,000 soldiers in 751 and with 100,000 in 754; Nanzhao defeated the first force at Xiaguan.

territoryChange.value: Expanded into Burma and Sichuan in the 800s; conquered by Kublai Khan’s Mongol army (1253).

alliancesRivals.value: Switched between Tang China and the Tibetan Empire: allied with Tibet from 752, then made peace with Tang in 794.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; skilled bronze casting and swordsmithing.

scienceEducation.value: Buddhist monasteries and Chinese learning; the Nanzhao Dehua stele (766) records the kingdom’s history.

openness.value: Open to Chinese, Tibetan and Indian influences.

communicationTransport.value: Mountain trails and pack-horse routes; bridges across deep river gorges.

religion.value: Buddhism (Azhali) was practised from about 821–824; the last Nanzhao king made it the official state religion.

languageWriting.value: Bai and Yi languages; Chinese characters.

artsArchitecture.value: The Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple at Dali and the long painted scroll of Buddhist images by Zhang Shengwen (1170s).

socialStructure.value: Royal and noble families, Buddhist clergy, farmers and herders, and slaves from captured peoples.

sharedIdentity.value: Bai and Yi peoples under Buddhist kings.

dailyLife.value: Wood and stone houses in lakeside villages; rice, fish and dairy food.

neighbours.value: Tang and Song China, the Tibetan Empire, the Pyu and Pagan kingdoms of Burma, and Annam.

ideasReligions.value: Buddhism shaped kingship: several Dali kings retired to become monks.

riseSignals.value: Piluoge united the Six Zhaos in 737 and founded Nanzhao; the Tang recognised him in 738 and the capital was set at Taihe in 739.

peakPeriod.value: Nanzhao conquered the Pyu city-states in the 820s, destroyed Halin in 832, raided Annan in 846 and occupied it again from 863 for three years, and attacked Chengdu in 869.

declineSignals.value: The Mongol invasion of 1253; the Duan family stayed on as local governors under the Mongols.

outcome.value: The Nanzhao royal family was murdered by Zheng Maisi in 902; Duan Siping seized power in 937 and founded the Dali Kingdom. The article does not state the Mongol conquest year.
